title: The South Dakota Rag by Dee Cort Keith Hammitt (1913)
artist_name:
Dee Cort Keith Hammitt

DeeCort Hammitt was an accomplished musician, composer and bandleader from South Dakota. Early in his career he wrote this rag named for his home state, a creative and unusual rag which preceded his best-known composition by a number of years, "Hail South Dakota", which was adopted as the official state song of South Dakota in 1943. The same year he published this rag, 1913, he married Bessie Jane Durkee, and they went on to have a large family of eleven children. In 1921 he was appointed director of the Alcester Community Band, which grew to become of the official South Dakota State Band. They performed for President Calvin Coolidge in 1927. He also continued his career as a songwriter. In 1947 he and Bessie moved to Sacramento, California where he operated a music store business until his death in 1970 at age 77.

title: "Virginia Rag" (1907), by Sydney P. Harris
artist_name:
Sydney P. Harris

Sydney (sometimes spelled as Sidney) P. Harris was born in North Yorkshire in England, with the best estimate placing the year around 1871. His parents, sister and brother came to St. Louis, Missouri in the late 1870s. In 1880 Sydney is mentioned as being nine years old. He appeared on stage in 1892 playing the violin in St. Louis together with a pianist, Dorothea Stohlman. They married in 1896, but divorced in the early 1900s. He was present at the earthquake in San Francisco in 1906 and his story and experience from there were published in newspapers all over America. There he was referred to as “the composer of The Cavalier” (his 1905 march). This march must have been very popular, perhaps because it was also played by Sousa’s band. In 1907 "Virginia Rag" was published by Sydney P. Harris Co. with an address in New York City; it was re-released from the same location in 1909. In 1908 he married again to Marie Flanelly, in Michigan, but claimed to have been born around 1880. In years between 1910 and 1940 he was living in Detroit, listed as musician and music publisher, and gave several different years as his year of birth. He died in Detroit in 1944 mentioned as a musician born in 1875. And to top it off, his tombstone laid by his widow Marie states a birth year of 1884!

title: "Indigo Blues" (1918), by Isham Jones
artist_name:
Isham Jones 

Isham Jones (1894-1956) was still an up-and-coming composer when he wrote this great fox trot in 1918. Working from Chicago as a musician and bandleader, he'd already had one big hit, "You're in the Army Now" from 1917. He and his Isham Jones Orchestra hit it big all throughout the 1920s and into the 1930s with a remarkable string of #1 hit songs and recordings and many other top 10 tunes. He recorded extensively with Brunswick and later other labels, recognized as one the greatest dance bands of the era.

title: The Technic Touch Rag by Harold B. Knox (1913)
artist_name:
Harold Blaine Knox 

Harold Blaine Knox (1892-1936) was a talented musician originally from Clare, Michigan where he worked as a theatre pianist. He moved to Portland, Oregon around 1912 where he worked for The Oregonian newspaper and met his fiancée, Hazel Johnston, whom he married in 1914. He performed as a violinist and pianist while there and later led an orchestra and taught large classes of music students, working as a theatre organist in Sedro-Woolley north of Seattle, Washington. At some point Harold and Hazel divorced. In the early 1930s, he and his orchestra performed on ocean liners. After several trips to Alaska, he accepted work in Juneau, Alaska, where he died in 1936, leaving a son and a daughter. “Departed will be remembered as a young man of exceptional musical talent.” (Bio info with thanks to Musescore researcher Erlingl.)
H. Kirkus Dugdale was a music publisher based in Washington DC who accepted musical scores for publication from all over. By 1914 he was forced out of business for not always honoring the paid contracts he made with composers. But before that happened he was able to publish a lot of interesting scores, including a number of rags, that otherwise may have never been printed. This fascinating rag was one of them, published by Dugdale in 1913.
